newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: OLYMPICS-IOC HIT BY SCANDAL OVER KILLER DRUG.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-IOC HIT BY SCANDAL OVER KILLER DRUG.

text.p: The IOC was embroiled in a major drug controversy on Tuesday when a senior doping official claimed a male athlete was thrown out of the Atlanta Olympics for admitting to taking the killer drug erythropoietin (EPO).

IOC medical commission vice-president Jacques Rogge said in a television interview that an Eastern Europe competitor had admitted to the IOC that he was taking the drug which is suspected to have killed 18 cyclists in Europe in the last 10 years.

The affair appeared to mark the first case in the Olympics involving one of the most dangerous substances in sport. But the IOC's most senior doping official, Prince Alexandre de Merode, denied that it had happened.

In an interview to be broadcast on Danish television later on Tuesday, Rogge said: "An athlete was expelled from the Olympic village after he confessed to the medical commission that he had used EPO."

"It was an athlete from an Eastern European country who was being investigated for another drug. During the interrogation he admitted that he had taken EPO, signed a form and was disqualified," he added in a tape of the broadcast made available to Reuters.
But asked to confirm the case after an IOC meeting here, de Merode said: "It never happened. There must be some misunderstanding. We never had an EPO case."

The IOC has yet to introduce a test for the dangerous substance whose abuse is believed to be widespread in cycling and could also be used to cheat in endurance events like rowing or cross-country skiing.

But this case in Atlanta has not been widely publicised. Olympic officials announced just two positive cases of drug abuse at the Games involving two female athletes who were banned for steroid abuse.
Rogge's comments seemed clear in the television interview which was made in October by the DR1 network and was due to be broadcast at 2100 GMT. The interview was in English.
De Merode said there had been a case in Atlanta where a team doctor had been talking to IOC medical officials and mentioned that there were some EPO around at a cycling training camp.
But he added: "There was never an athlete expelled."
EPO, which was first introduced in the mid-1980s to treat kidney disease, is one of the most dangerous drugs used by athletes who want to cheat their way to glory.
Some experts have dubbed it the drug used by athletes who live by the motto: "Better dead than second."
It stimulates the production of red blood cells which transport oxygen around the body -- a quick shot-in-the-arm which replaces expensive training at high altitude.

EPO is produced naturally in humans but if it enters the body artificially it can be fatal, making the blood thick and gluey and breaking down the entire circulatory system. This can lead to heart attacks.
"I believe athletes used EPO and growth hormones but that is my subjective opinion," Rogge said.
The IOC is working on a test for EPO but it cannot say whether it will have a test in place by next year's Winter Olympics in Nagano.

Olympic officials are also unlikely to be ready to test for human growth hormones -- the expensive designer drugs which are rapidly replacing muscle-building steroids as a short-cut to glory -- by the 2000 Sydney Summer Games.
